title: Anxiety: responding to a possible threat
description: Something that might be a threat appears, and it stays uncertain for a while. The episode follows the response in a brain with an anxiety disorder; the typical response shows the same moment in a brain without one. The same regions take part in both. What the research supports is a difference in how strongly some of them respond and in how much the control regions step in. Whether the response also lasts longer in an anxiety disorder was not covered by the sources read, so the two brains follow the same time course here.
caveat: The findings come from different kinds of study that were never run as one experiment: group comparisons of people with social anxiety, phobia, PTSD and other anxiety disorders; studies of healthy volunteers waiting for an unpredictable shock; recordings from electrodes in the amygdala; and studies where people were asked to rethink an upsetting image. Joining them into one continuous episode is a reconstruction. "Anxiety disorder" here is an average over several different diagnoses, which differ from one another. The hypothalamus and the body's stress hormones are left out because none of the sources read for this episode measured them in people.

phases.name: A possible threat
phases.caption: Something that might be a threat appears. The amygdala is among the first regions to react, possibly within a fraction of a second; how fast, and by what route, is disputed.
phases.typicalCaption: Something that might be a threat appears. The amygdala is among the first regions to react here too: this first response is ordinary.

phases.name: Alarm
phases.caption: The alarm spreads. The insula, which tracks the state of the body, and the cingulate and medial frontal cortex respond strongly, and the amygdala responds more than it would in a typical brain.
phases.typicalCaption: The insula and the cingulate and medial frontal cortex join in. The pattern is the same as in an anxiety disorder, only smaller.

order.rationale: Electrode recordings put the first amygdala response under a tenth of a second, while the wider response is measured with brain scans that cannot resolve events faster than seconds. That the amygdala leads is an inference; the order among the insula and cingulate is unknown.

phases.name: Waiting, not knowing
phases.caption: The threat stays uncertain. A small structure deep in the front of the brain, the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, holds a sustained response while the amygdala's own response fades. This is known mostly from animal studies, and no difference from the typical brain is shown at this step because none was found in the sources read.
phases.typicalCaption: While things stay uncertain the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis holds a sustained response, as the amygdala's own response fades. This is known mostly from animal studies.

citations.title: Contributions of the Central Extended Amygdala to Fear and Anxiety.
citations.quote: the BST shows a persistent hemodynamic response during the uncertain anticipation of noxious reinforcers, such as shock or aversive images, whereas the dorsal amygdala shows more transient responses

phases.name: Regulation
phases.caption: The frontal control regions that help rethink a situation are recruited less than in a typical brain, and the insula is more active while trying.
phases.typicalCaption: Frontal control regions engage as the situation is reappraised, and the amygdala quietens. The episode settles.

order.rationale: Deliberate rethinking takes seconds and, in the studies that measure it, people are asked to do it after the upsetting image has appeared. Placing it last follows that design; in life, regulation can begin earlier and overlap with the alarm.

regions.explanation: Responds to the possible threat and, on average, more strongly than in people without an anxiety disorder. How fast it responds, and by what route, is disputed: electrode recordings found responses to fearful faces within about 74 milliseconds, but other researchers argue the cortex does more of this early work than the fast-route account allows. Whole-brain analyses also often fail to detect the amygdala, so its size here is uncertain. It follows the same time course as in the typical brain, only larger: the sources read do not say whether it lasts longer.

regions.explanation: Holds a sustained response while a threat stays uncertain. The clearest evidence is from rodents, and little is known about it in people. Brain-scan studies in people do show a persistent response here during uncertain waiting, but the tidy split between a fast amygdala and a slow bed nucleus is contested: in monkeys, both are tied to sustained anxiety. It is drawn exactly as in the typical brain, because the sources read report no difference in anxiety disorders.

connections.explanation: Communication between the amygdala and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex tends to be weaker in more anxious people. The evidence is from brains at rest, not during an episode, and the clearest patient finding is in social anxiety with the neighbouring orbitofrontal cortex.
